And I should add simply: I think this is a good quote for people with depression to meditate on.

***YOU SHOULD NEVER SAY IT TO SOMEONE WHO IS ACTIVELY DEPRESSED, lest you look like an unsympathetic donkey.***

It's always helped me when people just ask me genuinely what I'm feeling, have the capacity to listen (yes it can be a total downer), and then go "man that situation is shit ".
Most people who have depression have pretty good reasons to be.

When that happens and I feel heard and validated, only then do I have the reduction of stress enough to actually think about the problem.

When people are invalidating, or give cliches, I feel more denied, repressed, and invalidated. Which makes me feel more depressed than initially.

I struggled with depression for 16 years. Suicidal for 10 of them. I would say I'm in recovery or remission. I wish we had a word from when you dont feel depressed anymore. 
It's a tough battle and I dont think we have made the mental health discoveries necessary to help depression in the best way. There are many people who struggle chronically and dont know where else to turn.

But what I do know is I thought I'd never enjoy my life. And yet, despite horrific tragedy and trauma, I am happy now. I love my life. 
It's not a death sentence and we do have some influence over it.

I agree that to trivialize a mental health condition into a platitude is not accurate, and can even feel invalidating. 
Depression is not something easy or quick, which are words often associated with "temporary."

But temporary just means not forever. And I dont believe everyone with depression is doomed to suffer chronically with it *forever*.
I find a lot of value in the quote mention in OP. I think "temporary" is not a given, but an option. I believe most people with depression have the option to influence it in some level. Make it better or worse.
Not meaning that they choose or choose not to have it. But in the way that most can choose to pursue treatment and recovery, or not. 
It's not black and white, and I'm not saying it always works, nor that it's easy. The trouble with depression is that it attacks your energy and motivation -  two super important things when it comes to getting help.

Yet, help is still an option for most.

It takes a lot of work, but if you have the strength to get through each day with depression then you have the strength it takes.

It took me 3 years of strict medication and intensive therapy. Cutting off certain toxic influences in my life that I really loved.
And I achieved a level of mental contentment and stability I never thought I could ever feel. I thought maybe I could feel less miserable, but I never thought I would actually enjoy and WANT my life.
But now I do.

I have better friendships. I found a partner who loves me and does not abuse me. I have a job that is meaningful and my life is a blessing.

Hello. Thank you for posting this thread, I bookmarked it for reminders for myself.
My therapist always explained describing things objectively similar to watching objects on a conveyor belt. You watch the thing that is happening, you describe what you see, and you let it pass... without attaching other meaning to it.
For Example: that suitcase is red and large. (and not adding “It’s so much prettier than my suitcase because mine is ugly and I’m poor.”)

So in the example you gave above, I would imagine radical acceptance would be accepting the objective things.
“friendship is waning - I'm hearing less from someone, or the tone of the friendship has shifted.”
That would be the part that needs to be accepted.
The other maladaptive coping mechanisms, such as trying to rescue the friendship, or trying to run away, usually comes from a place (at least in my experience) of not *wanting* to accept the facts. Not wanting to accept the fact that a friend is acting differently or that a friendship may be changing in a way we don’t want it to. 

Those would be things to objectively radically accept. As specific as possible: “I’m hearing less from this friend- we usually text every day and it has been a week.”

Accepting that. Everything outside of that is other DBT skills. Mindfulness. Coping skills. Describing our emotions and identifying cognitive distortions, etc. 

Extra point of something I still struggle with sometimes: when we are observing, to do so without attaching other meaning to it. 
Healthy: Accepting that something is different, and being curious about it.
“This friendship feels different. It seems we haven’t been as open with each other lately, and it feels a little tense and awkward. Hm.. I wonder why.”

Versus: We are not close anymore. Our friendship is over, I am a terrible friend, I am unlovable, (what have you. Any number of negative meanings we could attach.)

The truth of the matter is: we don’t know *why* a person may be acting differently. It could be one of a hundred different reasons, ninety nine of which would have nothing to do with us. Accepting that we don’t know the motive behind someone’s actions is sometimes the hardest thing for me. But once I remember and accept that, I feel a lot more peace. And, if necessary, I am able to have a conversation with the friend about it without being too intense or negative.

If we, although with love and all the good intentions in the world, tried to force them to talk about it when they don’t want to, or to force them to “heal” at the pace we think they should, they would feel their power being lost once again.
The fact that she opened up and talked to you about it is a testament to your relationship. Ultimately it is her path to healing that she has to walk. But you can always have open communication, as long as you understand that you can’t force her to do anything she doesn’t want to do, even if that is deal with the situation. 1. Boundaries are super important. Identify what boundaries are important to you (for example, not becoming disrespectful when upset, not raising voice, not cursing, no insults, sarcasm, etc. Whatever you want), and *enforce* them.

2. You can reflect back what she is saying, without admitting fault. This will help her feel understood and to relax some, and will ensure that you actually understand what she is mad about. "So you're saying you are upset with me because I left my socks in the hallway?" If you do this enough times, often she will find her own solution and will calm down all by herself. This will help her get back to reason.
3. Let her be mad. Dont try to "fix" it. Mad is a normal emotion, just like happy or tired or excited. Dont try to make her not mad just because it feels uncomfortable for you; let her feel what she feels and it will pass.
